extraction.name: OpenThoughts3-1.2M
extraction.description: A large-scale reasoning dataset for training language models on math, code, and science tasks through supervised fine-tuning. The dataset contains 1.2 million question-answer pairs with long reasoning traces generated by teacher models.
extraction.creator: OpenThoughts-Team
extraction.publisher: Stanford University, University of Washington, BespokeLabs.ai, Toyota Research Institute, UC Berkeley, UT Austin, UCLA, JSC, LAION, NYU, UNC Chapel Hill, ASU, Lila Sciences, Cornell Tech, TUM, Open-Ψ(Open-Sci) Collective
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were sourced from existing datasets and generated synthetically, then annotated with reasoning traces by teacher models (primarily QwQ-32B). The pipeline involved question sourcing, filtering, deduplication, multiple answer generation per question, and teacher model annotation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions sourced from multiple datasets including OpenMath-2-Math (math), StackExchange CodeGolf and OpenCodeReasoning (code), StackExchange Physics and Organic Chemistry PDFs (science), along with various other public datasets and synthetically generated questions.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were filtered based on difficulty or response length using LLM-based methods. Deduplication was applied using exact match or fuzzy string similarity. Multiple answers (16×) were sampled per question from teacher models.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered using LLM-based difficulty assessment or response length filtering. Deduplication removed duplicate questions using exact or fuzzy matching. Questions were sampled and annotated multiple times (16×) by teacher models to generate diverse reasoning traces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Reasoning traces and answers were generated by teacher models (primarily QwQ-32B, with earlier experiments using DeepSeek-R1). Each question was annotated multiple times (16×) to generate diverse responses. No human annotation was performed on the reasoning traces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, Gemini-2.0-flash-lite-preview-02-05
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Multiple answer filtering strategies were tested including majority consensus, GPT verification, and response length selection. Experiments showed that no filtering strategy significantly outperformed using all generated answers without filtering.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: QwQ-32B (primary teacher model), DeepSeek-R1 (earlier experiments), GPT-4o-mini (question filtering and verification), GPT-4.1-nano and GPT-4.1-mini (response length filtering)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is part of the OpenThoughts project with multiple generations released (OpenThoughts-114K, OpenThoughts2-1M, OpenThoughts3-1.2M). All datasets and models are available on openthoughts.ai.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work aims to democratize reasoning model development by creating open datasets, but also raises safety concerns as supervised fine-tuning on reasoning data degrades pre-existing safety alignment.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on math, code, and science domains with questions primarily from competitive programming, mathematics competitions, and academic sources. Performance varies by domain and question difficulty. The dataset may not generalize well to other reasoning domains.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to math, code, and science domains. Models trained on this data show degraded safety alignment. The dataset does not include reinforcement learning data. Generalization to held-out benchmarks varies, with some tasks showing limited improvement. The dataset may contain contamination risks despite decontamination efforts.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training: The dataset is designed for supervised fine-tuning of reasoning models on math, code, and science tasks. The resulting models achieve state-of-the-art performance on reasoning benchmarks including AIME, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond.

name.evidence: Scaling the pipeline to 1.2M examples and using QwQ-32B as teacher yields our OpenThinker3-7B model

description.evidence: OpenThoughts3-1.2M, the focus of this paper, is the culmination of the insights gained from the previous OpenThoughts datasets and our systematic exploration (Section 4) of the dataset pipeline design space... OpenThoughts3-1.2M contains 850,000 math, 250,000 code, and 100,000 science datapoints.

url.evidence: Our OpenThinker3-7B model can be found in https://huggingface.co/open-thoughts/OpenThinker3-7B, and our dataset can be found in https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-thoughts/OpenThoughts3-1.2M

creator.evidence: OpenThoughts-114K (OpenThoughts-Team, 2025) demonstrates the effectiveness of scaling strong dataset generation strategies.

inLanguage.evidence: Removing Non-English Answers: Ask GPT-4o-mini whether a provided answer contains only English.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The first step in our data generation pipeline is finding questions for each data domain. We can broadly categorize our question sourcing techniques into three types: (1) Fully synthetic – an existing LLM generates questions with little-to-no seed material... (2) Semi-synthetic – an LLM uses existing data sources such as CommonCrawl or FineWeb as seeds to form questions... (3) Non-synthetic – humans write the questions.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Our experiments cover 27 different question sources for code questions, 21 sources for math, and 14 sources for science... Questions from StackExchange, CodeForces, and other online forums... LLM-generated questions from existing datasets and text corpora.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: For code, CodeGolf questions from StackExchange and competitive coding questions from OpenCodeReasoning... For math, both LLM-generated questions in openmath-2-math and human-written questions in NuminaMath... for science, the highest-scoring question generation strategies are physics questions from StackExchange and LLM-extracted questions from organic chemistry textbooks

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: The two highest performing question filtering methods are difficulty-based filtering and response length filtering... We explore three degrees of deduplication strictness: no deduplication, exact match deduplication, and fuzzy deduplication using a threshold-based string similarity... we select the optimal strategy, which is exact deduplication with 16× answers per question.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Difficulty-based filtering asks an LLM (GPT-4o-mini) to assess the difficulty of each question, then retains the most difficult questions... response length filtering asks an LLM to respond to each question directly, then selects the questions with the longest LLM-generated responses... Our final pipeline uses 16× answers per question for all domains.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Across all domains, using QwQ-32B as a teacher model outperforms all other teacher models... Our final pipeline uses 16× answers per question for all domains. It uses exact deduplication for math and science and no deduplication for code.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Table 7 shows the result of each filtering method for math datasets... across all domains, the no-filtering strategy (training on all samples without controlling compute) led to performance similar to that of all other methods of filtering. This result suggests that the benefits of answer filtering are not significant enough to justify reducing the number of samples in the dataset

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: Our final pipeline uses 16× answers per question for all domains.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: Across all domains, using QwQ-32B as a teacher model outperforms all other teacher models... We use difficulty-based filtering with GPT-4o-mini for code questions, and response length filtering with GPT-4.1-mini for math and science questions.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: We are launching the OpenThoughts project to create state-of-the-art open reasoning datasets... Beginning with BespokeStratos-17K, we have progressed through four generations of releases, culminating in OpenThoughts3-1.2M... All of our datasets and models are available on openthoughts.ai.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The goal of the OpenThoughts project is to demystify the SFT data curation process and gain a deeper understanding of what contributes to a strong reasoning SFT dataset... we observe that supervised fine-tuning on reasoning inadvertently degrades the pre-existing safety alignment of Qwen2.5 models... These findings underscore the challenge of balancing safety and utility in reasoning models

rai:dataBiases.evidence: OpenThoughts3-1.2M contains 850,000 math, 250,000 code, and 100,000 science datapoints... Questions sourced from competitive programming (CodeForces, ICPC), mathematics competitions (AIME, AMC, Olympiads), and academic science sources... some benchmarks are saturating (AMC23, MATH500) at the largest scale, and others do not respond to scale (HLE).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: This work has several limitations. We did not explore datasets for reinforcement learning... Within the SFT realm, we did not explore the use of staged SFT or curriculum learning... OpenThinker3-7B was trained without any explicit safety-tuning or alignment-focused data, which likely contributes to its degraded safety performance... some benchmarks are saturating (AMC23, MATH500) at the largest scale, and others do not respond to scale (HLE).

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: OpenThinker3-7B is the best open-data reasoning model at the 7B scale, regardless of optimization algorithm choice (SFT, RL, or both)... OpenThinker3-7B achieves state-of-the-art results: 53% on AIME 2025, 51% on LiveCodeBench 06/24-01/25, and 54% on GPQA Diamond
